summary: This standards-track memo defines a MIB module for managing tunnels of any type over IPv4 and IPv6 networks. Other MIB modules can extend it for specific tunnelling protocols.

eli5.summary: A tunnel carries packets inside other packets. This document defines the dials for checking and managing such tunnels remotely.

questions: what is the ip tunnel mib
how to create a tunnel with snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects for managing tunnels of any type over IPv4 and IPv6, with one table to inspect them and one to create them.

tldr.problem: Many tunneling protocols exist (GRE, IP-in-IP, L2TP and others), and the earlier tunnel MIB in RFC 2667 handled only IPv4 endpoint addresses.
tldr.mechanism: Each tunnel gets a logical interface row in the Interfaces MIB plus a row in a Tunnel Interface Table. A second table, indexed by endpoint addresses, encapsulation method and an ID, lets a manager create tunnels and find their interface index.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2667. It deprecates the IPv4-only objects in favor of IP-version-agnostic ones and adds an IANA-maintained tunnel type convention.

today: RFC 4087 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2005 that obsoletes RFC 2667. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Tunnel MIB
sections.content:
The IETF has specified many tunneling protocols. RFC 4087 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module, TUNNEL-MIB, for managing tunnels of any type over IPv4 and IPv6. The RFC names, among others, GRE, IP-in-IP, Minimal Encapsulation, L2TP, PPTP, L2F, UDP, ATMP and IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels.

The module is generic. Extension MIB modules may add protocol-specific objects, or security-specific ones such as IPsec. Tunnels over non-IP networks are not supported, though other MIB modules may cover them.

The module follows SMIv2 and is accessed through SNMP, as the Internet-Standard Management Framework describes.
sections.eli5: Many different kinds of tunnels exist. This document gives one common set of dials that works for all of them.

sections.title: Two Tables, One Deprecated
sections.content:
The module contains two current tables and one deprecated table. The Tunnel Interface Table (tunnelIfTable) holds information on the tunnels known to a router. The Tunnel Inet Config Table (tunnelInetConfigTable) can be used for dynamic creation of tunnels, and also maps endpoint addresses to the current interface index.

The tunnelConfigTable from RFC 2667 mapped IPv4 endpoint addresses to interface indexes. It is now deprecated in favor of the Inet version.
sections.eli5: One table is the list of tunnels that exist. The other is the order form for making a new tunnel, and it also tells you which tunnel you got.

sections.title: Tunnels and the Interfaces MIB
sections.content:
Each logical interface, physical or virtual, has an ifEntry in the Interfaces MIB (RFC 2863). A tunnel is handled by creating a logical interface for it. The ifStack table then correlates that interface with the interfaces on which the tunnel's local IPv4 or IPv6 addresses are configured. The ifType of a tunnel should be tunnel (131), and an entry in the IP Tunnel MIB exists for every ifEntry of that type.

The ifRcvAddressTable usage can be defined by the MIB modules for the encapsulation below the network layer. If none is specified, there is one entry for the tunnel interface, holding the local address used for encapsulation and decapsulation.

The RFC explains why there are two tables. Interface indexes are normally chosen by agents and may change across restarts, so allowing row creation directly in a table indexed by ifIndex would complicate things. Instead, the creation table is indexed only by values the manager controls: the endpoint addresses and the encapsulation protocol, plus a manager-chosen ID for protocols such as L2F that allow multiple tunnels between the same endpoints.
sections.eli5: Every tunnel shows up as its own pretend network cable in the device's list of connections. That way the usual tools can count its traffic like any other cable.

sections.title: The Tunnel Interface Table
sections.content:
Each row of tunnelIfTable describes one configured tunnel and is indexed by ifIndex. The current objects are:

  • tunnelIfEncapsMethod: the encapsulation method, of type IANAtunnelType.
  • tunnelIfHopLimit: the IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit for the outer header, from 1 to 255, where 0 means copy it from the payload's header.
  • tunnelIfSecurity: none, ipsec or other.
  • tunnelIfTOS: how the 6 high bits (the differentiated services codepoint) of the outer header are set. -1 copies them from the payload, -2 invokes a traffic conditioner, and 0 to 63 sets the value directly.
  • tunnelIfFlowLabel: how the IPv6 Flow Label is set, where -1 means a traffic conditioner is invoked.
  • tunnelIfAddressType, tunnelIfLocalInetAddress and tunnelIfRemoteInetAddress: the address type and the outer-header source and destination. An unknown address is 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 or :: for IPv6, and the remote address is also unspecified when the tunnel is not point-to-point, such as 6to4.
  • tunnelIfEncapsLimit: the maximum number of additional encapsulations allowed, from 0 to 255, where -1 means no limit apart from packet size.

The older IPv4-only tunnelIfLocalAddress and tunnelIfRemoteAddress are deprecated.
sections.eli5: Each tunnel has a little card of settings: what kind of tunnel it is, where it starts and ends, how many hops its outer envelope may travel, and whether it is protected.

sections.title: Creating Tunnels
sections.content:
A row in tunnelInetConfigTable is indexed by address type, local address, remote address, encapsulation method and an ID. The ID tells apart multiple tunnels of the same method between the same endpoints. If the protocol allows only one tunnel per pair of endpoints (such as GRE or IP-in-IP), the ID is 1. For protocols such as L2F, the manager picks any ID that does not conflict, such as a random number.

To create a tunnel, the manager sets tunnelInetConfigStatus to createAndGo. If the ID is already in use, the agent returns inconsistentValue, and the manager picks a new pseudo-random number and retries. The agent then assigns an interface index in an implementation-dependent way and instantiates matching rows in the ifTable and tunnelIfTable. The row becomes active as soon as the index is assigned, whether or not the interface is operationally up. Deleting the row deletes those corresponding rows.

The row also shows the assigned index in tunnelInetConfigIfIndex and has a tunnelInetConfigStorageType.

One limit applies: object OIDs have at most 128 sub-identifiers. If the local and remote addresses together exceed 110 octets, column instances cannot be accessed with SNMPv1, SNMPv2c or SNMPv3. IPv4 and IPv6 addresses never reach this limit.
sections.eli5: To get a new tunnel, you fill in the order form. If your tunnel number is already taken, you pick another random number and try again. Once it is accepted, the tunnel appears in the list of connections.

sections.title: The IANA Tunnel Type Convention
sections.content:
The RFC introduces a new IANA-maintained textual convention, IANAtunnelType, added to the IANAifType-MIB. Its assignment policy matches that for IANAifType values. New types of tunnels over IPv4 or IPv6 should not get new IANAifType values. They should get IANAtunnelType values and reuse the interface type tunnel(131).

Earlier, tunnel types that were not point-to-point could not be expressed properly, so they were given IANAifType values. IANA deprecated sixToFour(215) as an IANAifType in favor of sixToFour(11) as an IANAtunnelType. The initial values, from other(1) to teredo(14), are listed in Appendix A.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of tunnel kinds, each with a number. New kinds are added to this tunnel list instead of getting their own new connection type.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The writable and creatable objects may be sensitive. Unauthorized write access could create or change tunnels, causing denial of service or redirecting packets to an arbitrary destination. Unauthorized read access to the tunnel endpoint addresses, or to any object in the config tables, would reveal the tunnel topology.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with its cryptographic mechanisms and says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Even on a secure network such as one using IPsec, nothing controls who may read or change the objects.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can press the buttons could redirect your mail or shut it off, and anyone who can read the dials could see how your tunnels are laid out. So only trusted people should get access.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2667
sections.content:
The IPv4-specific objects were deprecated, including the local and remote address objects, the tunnelConfigTable and the tunnelMIBBasicGroup. IP-version-agnostic replacements were added, including tunnelIfAddressType, the Inet address objects and the tunnelInetConfigTable.

The new Inet address objects are read-write rather than read-only. Descriptions of existing objects such as tunnelIfTOS were updated to cover IPv6, and tunnelIfFlowLabel was added for tunnels over IPv6. The encapsulation method was an INTEGER and is now the IANA-maintained textual convention.
sections.eli5: The old version only understood the older kind of addresses. The new version understands both old and new ones, and the old parts are marked as retired.
